For lack of having played a major political role, and especially for lack of a publication of her main writings, the collective memory continues to ignore the existence of this extraordinary woman who nevertheless belongs to the small number of authentic intellectuals of the time and to the very exclusive club of princess philosophers. Very in love with the young Prince Louis-Eugène of Württemberg, described as original, she had suffered from his distance from the Court by Marie-Thérèse who did not want to hear about marriage. It is therefore probable that Isabelle's friendship and tenderness came at just the right time to console her and that little by little she got caught up in the game... of love. Five months younger than Isabelle _ she is a lovely young girl, with a well-shaped, fine figure, a pleasant face, beautiful blue eyes, answer: how far did this homosexual relationship go and, above all, was it experienced as such by the two protagonists? When Isabelle writes: “I kiss you with all my strength, but no longer with my chin”, or: “I kiss you everything you let fuck”, or finally: “It could well happen that we kiss until we are exhausted”, we have little doubt about the desire that these words express. Especially since on several occasions, she evokes their couple in a heterosexual mode, she in the role of the man and Marie-Christine in that of the woman. It remains to be seen whether the two women are fully aware of breaking a ban. Certainly, Isabelle shows great concern to keep their meetings secret and warns Marie-Christine: "[...] I hope you remember the word given [...] never just talk about it, because there is nothing in the world so infamous 137 as going against nature." But female homosexuality, which did not yet have a name in the 16th century, did not suffer from the stigmatization and condemnation that surrounded “queerism” and infamy. Sapphic loves seemed more to do with female friendship than with sexuality, and caresses between women appeared to be innocent games of hands. Moreover, in the following century, the prudish Queen Victoria would again affirm to her Prime Minister that female homosexuality cannot exist... This was perhaps the opinion of the two women and those around them. After all, Isabelle's letters were not burned upon her death. They were even read by Marie-Christine's loving husband, Prince Albert of 139 Saxe-Teschen, who found absolutely nothing to complain about. On the contrary, after her death, he piously preserved them as the testimony of an exceptional friendship between his wife and an unparalleled princess. She had greatly impressed him, as we can judge from this passage from her Memoirs: “This truly astonishing woman who was not yet twenty years old [when she arrived in Vienna] was gifted not only with all the qualities of the heart which made her estimable, but she also brought together all the knowledge and talents directed the artists she had worked with, and she wrote with ease and an unusual spirit. [...] Too reserved in the rest of her remarks, her physiognomy denoted, despite all the attention she took to hide it, a tendency to dark ideas which proved that she was not perfectly happy, and on the subject of which she never explained herself very clearly, even towards the people in whom she placed the greatest confidence. 25° THE OBSESSION OF DEATH The prince of Saxony was right. Isabelle had difficulty concealing her terrible fears of death, perhaps inherited from the blood of the Bourbons. She is consumed by the presentiment of her imminent end which provokes in her an insurmountable attraction-repulsion. Shortly after his disappearance, Count Zinzendorf reported in his Journal a confidence that Princess Esterhazy had from Isabelle's first lady-in-waiting, Countess Erdédy, who was very close to her. “[Isabelle] was so struck by the death of her mother [in December 1759], that she threw herself on her knees to pray to God to make her know how much she had to live. Thereupon, she claims to have heard four knocks; straight away she said that she would live four days; when these were over, four weeks, then four months; finally when all this was over, she maintained that she would only live until her twenty-second year. She resolved to become a nun but, when the Archduke asked for it, her confessor persuaded her to accept this option, adding that she was made to make her subjects happy. When Madame d’Erddédy came take her to [Milan?], she said to him: “I think you will have a good mistress, but you will only have her for four years.” She always retained this apprehension in the middle of her wedding ceremonies, in the middle of the Court. Sometimes she was cheerful, she was pranking, but all of a sudden she regained her seriousness, and began to daydream.” It is clear that she actually died four years less nine days after her mother... The letters to Marie-Christine are full of references to the death which will separate her from her beloved. As early as 1761, she wrote to him: “I thought about death again last night, but the more I think about it, the less I can get to grips with this idea, since it will be a separation from you and I am convinced that it would not be possible to find someone who could replace me with their friendship for 142 you.”The terrible agony of her sister-in-law Jeanne in December 1762 accentuates his obsession and his contradictions: “Why am I not in his place? Death is a good thing. I swear to you that in my life I have never thought about it more seriously than at this hour. I represented all the horrors at leisure and in detail, but I also admit that this, far from disgusting me, made me want to die more than ever. God sees my heart, [...] he reads the regret I have for not having benefited from his graces and the desire to leave a life in which, despite my efforts, I will offend him every day. [...] Lamort would be dear to me. The only regret of leaving you is the pain that I can almost overcome.” Torn between her romantic passion and her spirituality, Isabelle fights with all her strength to make the latter triumph. This is evidenced by her Christian Meditations, written during her annual retreat, where she calls out to herself: “You feel every day that grace is withdrawing, that the danger is becoming greater than you; get out of such a dangerous state; finally wake up! [...] Why do you persist in your damnation? Deign, Lord, to help me [...] from now on it is only you that I want to love.” Yet his objurgations remain a dead letter. “I start the day thinking about the object I adore [...] and I end the day with the idea of ​​the one I am constantly occupied with. But why can't I think the same about God? He is invisible and we cannot love what we cannot see. [...] Alas! Nature [...] trains me to constantly take care of the one who charms me, and to forget the 145 Lord for her.” At the beginning of 1763, Isabelle began to prepare Mimi for her disappearance, which she thought was imminent: “I cannot absolutely, and whatever I do, conceive that I would have to see another year pass, and if there were certain announcements of death, it would have to be one. I would take it if I believed myself Holy enough for an inspiration from Heaven, because such a strong, calm feeling is rare [...]. I can say that it seems to me that a secret voice is announcing it to me. » But as she is not a saint, she thinks that her head is spinning and that she is “close to going crazy”. Without transition, she does a pirouette and announces that she is going to begin the painting requested by Marie-Christine... At the end of September 1763, when the Court left Schonbrunn, she remained the last with Marie-Christine. According to Zinzendorf, she expressed her melancholy with these words: “Ah, if only we could stay in Schonbrunn! » Then, before leaving: “She often returned to her room, saying “Goodbye my room, goodbye my armchair, we will not see each other again.” Of course, Marie-Christine wanted to hear nothing of these morbid comments and we know from Isabelle's responses that she often reproached him for his "dark thoughts". But the latter, sure of what she was doing, looked for a way to help him face the ordeal of his death and above all to live better afterwards among his family. Her happiness and her destiny as archduchess were at stake. She made a will addressed to Mimi alone, called “Advice to Mary”, where she reveals to her the secrets of her incredible ascendancy over the emperor and empress. In another text, she introduces him to the psychology of the future Emperor Joseph II, on whom his life will depend. It is perhaps these documents of around twenty 149 pages, classified among her correspondence, which best reveal the finesse and depth of Isabelle's psychology. But also a faculty of anticipation worthy of great a chess player and, let’s say it, an astonishing calculating duplicity.

This is therefore the first time that we have presented a complete edition of this correspondence, at least without the spirit of censorship. It consists of two hundred and sixty-three sheets, archived without the slightest chronological concern, the majority of which has been numbered from 99 to 318. In total, there are one hundred and ninety-four letters and notes from Isabelle and a single letter from Marie-Christine which is a portrait of her correspondent. The whole thing extends over a period of more than three years: from July 1760 to November 1763. The difficulties inherent in this manuscript are of different orders. First, Isabelle de Bourbon-Parma, who speaks four languages, uses French and German here, but often with inappropriate expressions. Although the vast majority of letters are written in French, they are often peppered with Germanisms and incorrections. Furthermore, as was common at that time, she ignored the art of punctuation. All things which do not make it easy to understand. We therefore chose to modernize the spelling as well as establish the punctuation. A small minority of letters and notes (sometimes written in tiny handwriting on very small pieces of paper) in German from the 16th century were translated almost literally and printed in italics to better distinguish them from French. Water, stains or ink stains make certain words or groups of words completely illegible. In this case, we indicate it with a note. But the major problem with this correspondence is above all of a chronological order. The vast majority of letters are undated. This absence of dating is the source of inevitable errors on our part. It is obvious that those which do not refer to any particular event are, so to speak, undatable. When possible, we relied on their emotional tone to choose Marie-Christine, in possession of Isabelle. These have remained untraceable to this day, probably because people wanted to make them disappear. Two notes from Empress Marie-Thérèse to the faithful Countess Erdédy, written just after Isabelle's death, seem to point in this direction. In the first, she states that her daughter-in-law had recommended all her papers to her, because “everything was not visible to him [Joseph]”. [...] Of all the services rendered, this is one of the greatest that you can render to me and my family.” Thank God, the letters addressed to Marie-Christine escaped this search...
